sourceEvidence.title: EGR Valve/Cooler Failure
sourceEvidence.howToFix: Clean or replace EGR valve (03L131501K). Inspect EGR cooler (03L131512AF) for leaks - coolant loss can indicate internal cooler failure. Regular intake cleaning helps prevent carbon buildup. Use quality diesel fuel. The EGR cooler removal process is documented at myturbodiesel.com for CBEA/CJAA engines.

sourceEvidence.title: Diesel Injector Failure
sourceEvidence.howToFix: Use quality diesel fuel. Have injectors tested with VCDS if symptoms appear - check injection quantity deviation. Replace failed injectors individually (03L130277A, Bosch 0445116030). Always replace injector seals when removing injectors. Injector seal kit includes copper washer (WHT000884 bottom O-ring, 059130119 top O-ring, 059130519 seal ring). Consider professional injector cleaning service before full replacement.

sourceEvidence.title: Turbocharger Failure
sourceEvidence.howToFix: Regular oil changes with VW 507.00 spec diesel oil are critical - the turbo depends on clean oil for bearing lubrication. Replace turbo if failed using OEM BorgWarner unit (03L253056). Always replace the turbo oil feed line (03L145771) and oil return line (03G145736F) with new gaskets (03L145757Q oil return gasket) when replacing the turbo. Let engine idle 30-60 seconds before shutdown to allow turbo to cool down.

sourceEvidence.title: Panoramic Sunroof Drain Tube Clogging
sourceEvidence.howToFix: Clear all four sunroof drain tubes using compressed air or a flexible cleaning wire. Clean the sunroof channel tray. Inspect and replace any cracked drain tube connections at the roof corners.

sourceEvidence.title: Rear Upper Shock Mount Bushing Wear
sourceEvidence.howToFix: Replace rear upper shock mount bushings. Consider replacing rear shocks at the same time if over 80,000 miles. Bilstein B4 or Sachs OE replacements are recommended. Realign rear suspension after service.

sourceEvidence.title: ZF 6HP26 Automatic Transmission Torque Converter Shudder and Failure
sourceEvidence.howToFix: Diagnosis typically includes scanning the transmission control module for ratio and converter clutch faults, checking fluid condition, and measuring slip values during road testing. Repairs range from fluid/filter service and valve body work to torque converter replacement or full transmission rebuild if clutch debris has contaminated the unit. Using the correct ZF Lifeguard fluid and adapting the transmission after repair is commonly recommended.

sourceEvidence.title: Timing Chain Tensioner Failure (2.0 TFSI Engine)
sourceEvidence.howToFix: PREVENTIVE REPLACEMENT: Replace timing chain, tensioners, and guides at 80,000-100,000 miles BEFORE rattling starts ($2,000-$3,000). If rattling has started, DO NOT delay—chain can jump at any moment. Repair requires removing front engine cover, water pump, thermostat. Labor is 8-12 hours. Use ONLY OEM Audi parts—aftermarket tensioners fail quickly. Change oil every 5,000 miles and check oil level weekly to prevent accelerated tensioner wear. If catastrophic failure occurs, engine replacement ($6,000-$10,000) is often more cost-effective than rebuild. 2021+ Q3 models have updated parts and are more reliable.

sourceEvidence.title: Supercharger Bearing Failure and Boost Leaks (3.0T)
sourceEvidence.howToFix: Worn bearings: Supercharger rebuild with new bearings ($1,500-2,500) or replacement supercharger ($3,000-5,000). Bypass valve: Replace supercharger bypass valve ($300-600). Boost leaks: Inspect all boost hoses/clamps, replace cracked hoses ($150-400). Use OEM Audi or quality aftermarket (INA) supercharger bearings. AudiWorld recommends catch can installation ($300-500) to reduce oil vapor damage to supercharger.

sourceEvidence.title: Water Pump and Thermostat Failure (Overheating)
sourceEvidence.howToFix: IMMEDIATE if overheating: Pull over, turn off engine, DO NOT continue - engine damage occurs in minutes. Preventive: Replace water pump/thermostat assembly at 60k-80k miles ($800-1,500) to avoid catastrophic failure. Failed pump: Replace water pump/thermostat ($800-1,500). If overheated: Cylinder head inspection, possible head gasket replacement ($2,500-5,000). Use OEM Audi or premium Geba/Meyle parts.

sourceEvidence.title: Front Brake Rotor Corrosion and Premature Pad/Rotor Wear
sourceEvidence.howToFix: For light surface rust, normal braking usually clears it; for noise, refinish or replace rotors and fit OEM-spec pads with proper bedding-in. Apply high-temp anti-seize/lubricant on contact points and ensure caliper slides move freely. Replace warped or deeply corroded rotors in axle sets.

sourceEvidence.title: Panoramic Sunroof Water Leak Into Cabin (TSB)

sourceEvidence.title: A/C Compressor Failure Requiring Engine-Out Repair (4.2 V8)
sourceEvidence.howToFix: A/C COMPRESSOR REPLACEMENT: Requires ENGINE REMOVAL on the V8 model. Total repair cost $5,000-$8,000 ($1,000-$1,500 for parts, $4,000-$6,500 for labor). When the engine is out, strongly recommended to also address: motor mounts, clutch inspection, and any other components that benefit from engine-out access. ALTERNATIVE: Some specialty R8 shops have developed methods to access the compressor with partial disassembly (removing subframe) rather than full engine removal, potentially reducing labor to $3,000-$4,000. PREVENTION: Run the A/C regularly (even in winter for 5-10 minutes monthly) to keep compressor seals lubricated.

sourceEvidence.title: Turbo Wastegate Rattle and Carbon Buildup
sourceEvidence.howToFix: Diagnose the concern by scanning for boost-control and turbocharger actuator faults, logging requested vs. actual boost, and physically checking both turbo wastegate linkages/actuators for free play or rattle at idle; also inspect intake valves with a borescope for carbon accumulation. Repair typically involves replacing the affected turbocharger assembly or wastegate actuator hardware where serviceable, then performing actuator basic settings/adaptation with a factory-capable scan tool; if carbon buildup is significant, perform walnut blasting of the intake valves and intake-port cleaning. On the 4.0T, labor is substantial because of turbocharger access in the hot-V, so expect roughly $3,500-$8,000+ for turbo-related repairs depending on whether one or both units are replaced, plus about $600-$1,200 for carbon cleaning.

sourceEvidence.title: B6/B7 4.2L V8 Timing Chain Tensioner Failure
sourceEvidence.howToFix: Diagnose by scanning for cam/crank correlation faults (commonly P0011, P0021, P0016-P0018), listening for prolonged chain rattle on cold start, and confirming camshaft adjustment values with VCDS or equivalent; severe cases may also show worn guide material in the oil pan. The proper repair is engine/transmission removal and replacement of the full rear timing service components: primary and secondary chain tensioners, chain guides/rails, timing chains as needed, cam adjuster hardware, seals/gaskets, and often related wear items such as valve cover gaskets and clutch or rear main seal while access is available. Because the timing set is mounted at the rear of the 4.2L V8, this is a labor-intensive job typically requiring precise locking tools and timing setup, with independent shop costs commonly around $4,000-$7,000 and dealer repairs often higher. Continuing to drive with startup rattle or timing faults risks chain jump and catastrophic valve-to-piston engine damage.

sourceEvidence.title: EA839 2.9T V6 Water Pump Internal Leak and Overheating (C8 S7)
sourceEvidence.howToFix: If coolant loss or an overheating warning appears, stop driving and have the cooling system pressure-tested. Replace the water pump with the updated 6-bolt-pulley revised unit, ideally as a combined water-pump-and-thermostat module, and inspect the vacuum solenoid valve (N649) for coolant contamination since it is commonly damaged by a leaking pump. Replace coolant and verify the vacuum control circuit operates correctly after repair. Affected owners should check eligibility under the EA839 water-pump class action.

sourceEvidence.title: Front Control Arm Bushing and Ball Joint Failure (C7 Suspension)
sourceEvidence.howToFix: Inspect all front control arms for play in the bushings and ball joints. Replace worn arms — many owners do the full front control-arm set (commonly a 16-piece kit covering both sides) to avoid repeat visits since the labor overlaps. Critical install notes: torque the bushing bolts at ride height (not with the suspension hanging) to avoid pre-loading and destroying the new bushings, and perform a four-wheel alignment afterward.

sourceEvidence.howToFix: Pull misfire counts per cylinder to localize the fault. Inspect/replace failed or leaking injectors and renew injector seals; replace spark plugs and any weak coils as a set. Confirm fuel trims return to normal and clear codes; address intake carbon if present.

sourceEvidence.title: Ignition Coil Pack Failure Causing Misfires (4.0T V8)
sourceEvidence.howToFix: Confirm the failing cylinder, then swap the suspect coil to another cylinder to verify the fault follows the coil. Replace the failed coil; best practice on the 4.0T is to replace all eight coils and the spark plugs as a set since the access labor is shared and mixed-age coils tend to fail in sequence. Use OE or quality OE-equivalent coils (the 4.0T uses the 079905110-series coil). Inspect spark plugs for fouling/oil that could indicate a secondary issue.

sourceEvidence.title: Premature Motor Mount Failure (4.0T V8)
sourceEvidence.howToFix: Replace both engine mounts as a pair ($800-$1,500 for both, $1,500-$2,500 with labor). Always replace BOTH mounts simultaneously—if one has failed, the other is close behind. Use OEM Audi mounts for proper damping characteristics. Aftermarket solid mounts increase NVH (noise/vibration) significantly. INSPECT: Check transmission mount at the same time—it often wears concurrently. Replace transmission mount if showing signs of deterioration ($400-$800 additional).

sourceEvidence.title: D2 4.2 V8 Timing Belt and Tensioner Service (Interference Engine)
sourceEvidence.howToFix: Replace the timing belt as a complete kit — belt, tensioner, idler/guide rollers, and water pump — at or before Audi's interval (and by age regardless of mileage). Use genuine/OE-quality components and set cam/crank timing precisely with the correct locking tools; this is a front-of-engine ('service position') job. Inspect the exhaust-side chain tensioners while in there. Always confirm timing-belt history (with receipts) before buying a D2 S8; if unknown, do it immediately.

sourceEvidence.title: Front Suspension Control-Arm Bushing and Sway-Bar Link Wear (Clunking)
sourceEvidence.howToFix: Inspect the front control-arm bushings (look for cracked/missing rubber at the inboard mounts) and grab the sway-bar end links for play. Replace worn sway-bar links first (cheap, bolt-in) and the upper/lower control arms as needed — use OE Lemforder/genuine arms rather than cheap aftermarket, which owners report wears out faster. Perform a four-wheel alignment after any arm replacement. Doing the full front 'arm kit' at once is common practice on higher-mileage cars to avoid repeat labor.

sourceEvidence.title: High-Pressure Fuel Pump / Injector Internal Leak Causing Hard or No-Start (4.0T)
sourceEvidence.howToFix: Diagnose per TSB 2046724 with a fuel-pressure decay test to isolate a leaking HPFP versus leaking injectors. Replace the failed high-pressure pump(s) and/or the affected high-pressure injectors. Because accessing the hot-vee valley is labor-intensive, shops often bundle other 'while-you're-in-there' items (PCV, coolant lines). Change the oil afterward if fuel dilution occurred.

sourceEvidence.title: Adaptive Air Suspension Compressor and Air Spring Failures
sourceEvidence.howToFix: Same diagnostic and repair approach as SQ7 (shared 4M platform). Isolate the failed component: air springs ($800-$1,500 per corner), compressor ($1,200-$2,500), valve block ($500-$1,000), or height sensor ($200-$400). Always check for air leaks before replacing the compressor. Aftermarket air suspension components from Arnott/Strutmasters offer 40-50% savings over OEM. Annual inspection of air springs for cracking recommended, especially in hot climates where UV and heat accelerate rubber degradation.

sourceEvidence.title: Front Control Arm Bushings and Ball Joint Wear Causing Clunks and Uneven Tire Wear
sourceEvidence.howToFix: Inspect lower control arm rear bushings, front bushings, ball joints, and tie-rod ends for play or torn rubber. Repairs typically involve replacing complete control arms or pressing in upgraded bushings, followed by a four-wheel alignment. Addressing the issue early improves steering precision and prevents abnormal tire wear.
